newsitem.title: USA: Israeli envoy to U.S. optimistic about summit.
newsitem.headline: Israeli envoy to U.S. optimistic about summit.

text.p: Israel's envoy to the United States on Sunday said he expected the upcoming summit between the Israeli and Palestinian leaders to be a success, as both knew the stakes for U.S. President Bill Clinton were high.

"I believe this summit is not going to fail, and if you ask me how I can be that confident, nobody is going to dare to do this to President Clinton," Ambassador Eliahu Ben-Elissar told CNN from New York.

Ben-Elissar said the meeting, which will take place in Washington this week, would be a great success if it produced a pact between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to end recent violence and get peace negotiations back on track.
He praised Clinton for the "very, very courageous initiative" of hosting the summit, and said neither side wanted to walk away without some positive results.

Clinton, facing his Nov. 5 election showdown with Republican Bob Dole in just over five weeks, on Sunday announced that Netanyahu and Arafat would come to Washington for high-level meetings this week.
White House officials said they were tentatively scheduled to take place on Tuesday and Wednesday.

In calling for the summit, Clinton was seeking to stop five days of clashes in which 55 Palestinians and 14 Israelis have died following Israel's opening of an archaeological tunnel near Jerusalem's al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third-holiest site.

Ben-Elissar said the Palestinians had used the tunnel as "a pretext for using bloodshed as a political tool." He said the Israeli government had offered to meet with Arafat but he had refused. "We are still willing to go on," he said.

Asked whether Israel planned to withdraw its soldiers from Hebron, as agreed in previous Israeli-Palestinian accords, Ben-Elissar said actions by Palestinian police in the clashes over the tunnel had resulted in "a break of confidence."

He said Israel would negotiate with Arafat and the Palestinian Authority on the withdrawal and related security matters, but there were now serious questions about whether Palestinian police would be able to enforce security there.
